body.text: Subsection 127(5) of Canada's Income Tax Act lets taxpayers deduct earned SR&ED investment tax credits from federal Part I income tax otherwise payable. Credits are earned at 15% or, for qualifying CCPCs and eligible Canadian public corporations, 35% on up to $6 million of qualified expenditures; unused credits may be refunded or carried back three years and forward 20.

Canada’s research and development (R&D) tax incentive landscape underwent its most significant structural expansion in over a decade with the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Incorporating legislative measures first proposed in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement and expanded in the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget (Canada Strong Budget 2025), the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program now provides an enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) on up to $6 million of qualified expenditures annually (doubled from the former $3 million expenditure limit, generating up to $2.1 million in refundable federal cash credits per year on current expenditures) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, Bill C-15 broadened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historical $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million, introduced an elective three-year average gross revenue phase-out test ($15 million–$75 million), extended the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) alongside Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), and restored SR&ED eligibility for capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.

On the administrative and provincial fronts, the 2025–2026 cycle introduced equally consequential reforms that alter how Canadian businesses structure, document, and stack innovation funding. Effective April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process for Canadian corporations and partnerships with less than $25 million in annual gross business income, offering upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks (valid for up to three years) and halving post-filing expenditure review service standards from 180 days to 90 days. At the provincial level, the Gouvernement du Québec’s 2025–2026 Budget replaced eight legacy provincial R&D tax measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating them into the refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which pays 30% on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an employee-based exclusion threshold (at least $50,000) and 20% on excess spending. According to provincial program guides, Saskatchewan likewise doubled its refundable CCPC R&D expenditure ceiling from $1 million to $2 million at a 10% rate effective December 16, 2024, while Alberta removed the sunset clause on its two-tier Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (8% base rate and 20% incremental rate up to $4 million) in its 2025 Budget, making it a permanent fixture of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act.

body.text: 1. Legislative and Statutory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Structure under the Income Tax Act

The federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program is codified within the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act" or "ITA"), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945 (the "Regulations" or "ITR"). Rather than operating through a single statutory deduction or credit, the program delivers tax relief through two distinct, sequential statutory mechanisms that must be calculated separately on Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)).

First, Section 37 of the Act establishes the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures. Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may deduct current and (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada that are related to a business of the taxpayer, or related to a business actively carried on by a related corporation under subsection 37(1.1). Instead of being subject to the general capital expenditure prohibition in section 18 of the Act, allowable SR&ED expenditures enter a cumulative, running statutory pool. The taxpayer may deduct all or any portion of the available positive pool balance against business income in the current taxation year, or carry the unclaimed pool balance forward indefinitely to offset business income in any subsequent taxation year.

Second, Sections 127 and 127.1 of the Act govern the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC). Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9), a taxpayer earns an ITC calculated as a percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of the taxpayer's "qualified expenditures" and "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" for the taxation year. Under subsection 127(5), earned ITCs are first applied to reduce federal Part I income tax otherwise payable. Depending on the claimant's legal status and expenditure limit, unused ITCs are either refunded in cash under subsection 127.1(1) or carried back 3 taxation years and forward 20 taxation years to offset Part I tax in those periods.

A critical audit principle highlighted in CRA policy and practitioner guides is that "allowable SR&ED expenditure" (under Section 37) and "qualified expenditure" (under Section 127) are legally distinct terms that frequently diverge in dollar value. An expenditure can be 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool without generating a Section 127 ITC on the same base, or can generate a Section 127 ITC without ever entering the Section 37 deduction pool.

body.text: 1.2 Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

Every federal and provincial R&D claim in Canada turns on the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set out in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Originally housed in section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations before being moved into subsection 248(1) of the Act (with the French version further amended by Royal Assent on June 26, 2013), the definition operates on what the Tax Court of Canada in 1726437 Ontario Inc. v. The Queen (2012 TCC 376) described as a "catch and release" structure: a broad initial definition of qualifying scientific and technological investigation ("catch"), followed by an exhaustive list of eight permitted support activities, and bounded by seven mandatory statutory exclusions ("release"). Small businesses represent the majority of program participants, accounting for 65% of all SR&ED claims submitted in the 2025–2026 fiscal year.

Under subsection 248(1), "scientific research and experimental development" means systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, categorized across paragraphs (a) through (k) as detailed below:

headers: Verbatim Statutory Scope & CRA Operational Interpretation

cells: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view (e.g., studying a newly discovered virus in a laboratory setting to understand its molecular properties, typically published in scientific journals).

Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view (e.g., investigating immunological mechanisms to develop a vaccine exploiting the characteristics of a newly discovered virus).

Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, or (8) psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.
Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes.
Research in the social sciences or the humanities.
Prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas.
The commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process.
Style changes (such as user interface redesigns or aesthetic alterations).

body.text: In audit practice, distinguishing between eligible Paragraph (d) support work (such as "testing" or "data collection") and Paragraph (f) or (k) excluded work ("routine testing" or "routine data collection") turns entirely on the purpose of the activity. Support work is never SR&ED on its own. However, if computer programming, data collection, or testing is performed specifically to execute an experiment or validate a hypothesis aimed at resolving a scientific or technological uncertainty under paragraph (a), (b), or (c)—and the scope of that work is commensurate with the experimental needs—it qualifies under paragraph (d). Conversely, once the scientific or technological advancement is achieved by resolving the associated uncertainties, or the claimant determines the uncertainties cannot be resolved, or the project is terminated for any reason, the project completion date is reached and all subsequent coding, testing, or manufacturing ceases to be eligible.
1.3 Evolution of CRA Eligibility Guidance: From the Five Questions to the "Why" and "How" Requirements

The administrative framework used by the CRA to evaluate whether work satisfies subsection 248(1) has evolved through four distinct historical stages. Prior to 1985, administrative guidance relied on Interpretation Bulletin IT-439, which taxpayers criticized as insufficient to explain eligible industrial research and development. In May 1985, federal Budget papers amended the definition of "scientific research" to incorporate "experimental development," confirming that routine engineering and routine development remained excluded. On March 4, 1986, the Department of Finance confirmed three core pillars—scientific or technological advancement, scientific or technological uncertainty, and systematic organization—which Revenue Canada and industry leaders codified in Information Circular IC 86-4 (and revised in IC 86-4R3 on May 24, 1994), followed by a 1992 legislative clarification confirming that experimental development includes incremental technological improvements.

Following Judge Bowman's landmark 1998 Tax Court of Canada judgment in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen ([1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520) and its endorsement by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen ([1999] 1 C.T.C. 132) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (2001 FCA 393), the CRA published its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy in 2012 (revised in 2015), which structured technical reviews around five sequential questions derived from Northwest Hydraulic. On August 13, 2021, following a 2020 modernization review, the CRA archived the 2012/2015 policy and published the modernized Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives. Rather than treating the five judicial questions as isolated mechanical checkboxes, the 2021 Guidelines consolidate the statutory test of subsection 248(1) into two mandatory requirements—the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement—while explicitly confirming that both the five questions and the two requirements derive from the unchanged statutory text of subsection 248(1).

How was the work conducted? The investigation must follow a structured, methodical scientific process directed specifically at overcoming the identified uncertainty.

body.text: A vital legal principle reinforced across both the CRA Guidelines and Tax Court jurisprudence is that commercial or technical success is not required. Because the advancement lies in the new scientific or technological knowledge gained, an experimental project that proves a hypothesis false or demonstrates that a technical approach cannot resolve the uncertainty qualifies for SR&ED up to the point the project was terminated, provided both the "Why" and "How" requirements were met.
1.4 Territorial Scope and Permissible Foreign SR&ED Work

As a general rule, the Section 37 deduction pool and Section 127 ITC apply only to SR&ED carried on in Canada (which, under subsection 37(1.3), includes Canada's exclusive economic zone). Under subsection 37(2), current expenditures on research carried on outside Canada are deductible in computing business income for the year, but they cannot be claimed on Form T661, do not enter the Section 37 indefinite carryforward pool, and do not earn Section 127 ITCs.

However, subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) provide a specific statutory exception allowing a claimant to include a limited amount of permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada inside its Canadian Section 37 pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures. Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), permissible foreign salary or wages are deemed to be an expenditure made in Canada equal to the lesser of Amount A and Amount B.
To qualify under Amount A (total eligible foreign SR&ED salary or wages under subsection 37(1.4)), the foreign work must satisfy all five cumulative statutory conditions:

items: The work was directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant (work performed by a foreign contractor or consultant never qualifies);
The employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred;
The work was related to a business of the claimant;
The foreign SR&ED work was an integral part of, and solely in support of, SR&ED work carried on in Canada by the claimant; and
The salary or wages paid were not subject to an income or profits tax from another country.

body.text: Under Amount B (subsection 37(1.5)), the permissible foreign amount is capped at 10% of the total salary or wages claimed for SR&ED carried on in Canada, as reported on Line 306 of Form T661. On Form T661, permissible foreign wages are split between Line 307 (employees other than specified employees) and Line 309 (specified employees), such that the combined sum of Line 307 and Line 309 cannot exceed 10% of Line 306, and for specified employees Line 309 cannot exceed 10% of Line 306 minus the amount claimed on Line 307.
2. Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Thresholds, and Corporate Eligibility (2026 Regime)
2.1 Basic (15%) vs. Enhanced (35%) ITC Rates and Eligible Taxpayers

Under subsection 127(9) of the Act, the federal SR&ED ITC is structured around two statutory rates. The Basic ITC Rate of 15% (reduced from 20% after 2013) applies to corporations that do not qualify for the enhanced rate (such as foreign-controlled subsidiaries and large corporations above the phase-out threshold), to qualified expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their annual expenditure limit, and to unincorporated claimants (individuals, certain trusts, and partners in a partnership, where the ITC is calculated at the partnership level and allocated to eligible partners under subsection 127(8)). The Enhanced ITC Rate of 35% applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the annual expenditure limit ($6 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; $3 million for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024).

Historically, only a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) could access the 35% enhanced rate. Consequently, Canadian technology and life-science firms that completed an Initial Public Offering (IPO) or became controlled by a public corporation immediately lost access to the 35% refundable credit, dropping to the 15% non-refundable rate. To remove this barrier to domestic public listings, Bill C-15 (enacted March 26, 2026, effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) created a new statutory corporate category: the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC). Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (published October 7, 2026), an ECPC is a public corporation listed on a designated stock exchange (or an eligible subsidiary within a consolidated group) that is resident in Canada and is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons—such that even if all shares owned by non-residents were instead owned by a single particular person, the corporation would still not be controlled by that particular person.
2.2 The $6 Million Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out ("Grind-Down") Mechanics

While the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement originally proposed raising the maximum annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3 million to $4.5 million, the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget (Canada Strong Budget 2025) increased the cap to $6 million, which was enacted into law by Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, retroactively effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

The nominal $6,000,000 expenditure limit ($3,000,000 for tax years beginning before December 16, 2024) must be shared among all associated CCPCs (allocated via Schedule T2SCH49 under subsection 127(10.3)) or across all members of a consolidated group of ECPCs included in consolidated financial statements. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 (expanded from the pre-December 16, 2024 taxable capital phase-out range of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000) under one of two statutory phase-out methods.

Under the Prior-Year Taxable Capital Method (the default rule for CCPCs), the expenditure limit begins to decrease when the associated group's taxable capital employed in Canada for the previous taxation year reaches $15,000,000, and becomes nil starting at $75,000,000. Under the Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Method (mandatory for ECPCs and elective for CCPCs), an ECPC's expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis when the corporation's (or consolidated group's) average gross revenue over the previous three fiscal years exceeds $15,000,000, becoming nil at $75,000,000. Crucially, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC or a group of associated CCPCs may elect to calculate its expenditure limit phase-out using the three-year average gross revenue method ($15 million to $75 million) in the same way as an ECPC instead of prior-year taxable capital.

Mathematically, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the annual Expenditure Limit (EL) as a function of the group's applicable phase-out metric M (either prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada or three-year average gross revenue) is:

For any group whose phase-out metric M lies between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, each $10 of M above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1. Other factors that reduce the expenditure limit include short taxation years and multiple taxation years ending within the same calendar year.

body.text: Several technical distinctions govern the application of this table. First, for both a standard CCPC (Rows 1 and 3) and an ECPC (Row 4), the 35% ITC earned on current expenditures up to the $6 million expenditure limit is 100% refundable (up to $2.1 million in cash), and the 35% ITC earned on capital expenditures up to the $6 million limit is 40% refundable, regardless of whether the corporation's prior-year taxable income kept it a "qualifying corporation". Second, a "qualifying corporation" is defined as a CCPC whose taxable income (combined with associated corporations) in the previous taxation year was not more than its qualifying income limit for the current year. If a CCPC is a qualifying corporation (Row 1), it can obtain a 40% cash refund on the 15% ITC earned on both current and capital qualified expenditures above the $6 million expenditure limit. By contrast, an ECPC (Row 4) or a CCPC that is not a qualifying corporation (Row 3) receives no cash refund (N/A) on the 15% ITC earned above the expenditure limit. Third, any portion of an ITC that is neither applied to reduce federal Part I tax payable in the current year nor refunded in cash may be carried back up to 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years (increased from 10 years for tax years ending after 2005).
Mechanics of the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Computed in Section C of Part 3 of Form T661, the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under subsection 37(1) operates as a cumulative running balance governed by specific statutory additions and reductions (Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, updated March 27, 2026):

Upon an acquisition of control of a corporation (or a new majority-interest beneficiary of a trust), the pool is reduced to nil, subject to reinstatement only if the business to which the expenditure related is continued for profit (or with a reasonable expectation of profit) and only to the extent of income from that same or a similar business.

body.text: Three operational rules govern the interaction between the Section 37 pool and taxable income. First, used or refunded federal SR&ED ITCs reduce the Section 37 pool in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(e). Because the opening pool balance at the beginning of a taxation year cannot be negative, any negative balance in the SR&ED pool at the end of a taxation year must be brought directly into net income for tax purposes in that year under paragraph 12(1)(v) (reported on Schedule T2SCH1), while paragraph 37(1)(c.1) adds that same amount back to the pool to reset the opening balance to nil ($0) for the subsequent taxation year (meaning no amount is reported on Line 450 of Form T661 in that subsequent year). Second, under subsection 37(4) and Regulation 2902(c), no deduction is allowed in the Section 37 pool for any expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED. Third, under paragraph 96(1)(e.1), a partnership cannot carry forward an amount in the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent fiscal period; the entire available pool must be deducted at the partnership level in computing partnership net income for the year.
3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
3.1 Election Between the Proxy Method and Traditional Method

To compute allowable SR&ED expenditures and qualified expenditures on Form T661, a claimant must elect each taxation year on Line 160 of Form T661 to use either the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) or the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)). This election applies to the entire claim for that taxation year and is irrevocable once the first Form T661 for that year is filed (though the taxpayer may choose differently in a subsequent taxation year). If a claimant does not select a method on Line 160, the CRA processes the claim using the Traditional Method.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically identify, track, or allocate overhead and other indirect expenditures on Form T661. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional substitute amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—in Part 5 of Form T661. Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA is 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base. Claimants and preparers must never use a 65% or 60% proxy rate; as noted in CRA policy and CPA audit warnings, the rate under Regulation 2900(4) was 65% up to 2012, 60% for 2013, and has been 55% since 2014.

Under the Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy (updated April 28, 2022), the PPA is subject to an Overall Cap on the PPA computed under Regulation 2900(6) using the statutory formula A − B − C, where A is the total amount deducted in computing business income for the year (including cost of goods sold), B is the sum of deductions claimed under sections 20, 24, 26, 30, 32, 37, 66 to 66.8, and 104 of the Act (such as Capital Cost Allowance [CCA], interest, and the Section 37 SR&ED deduction per Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), and C is the sum of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (such as building rent). This ensures the notional PPA cannot exceed the corporation's actual eligible overhead-type expenses for the year. While an ITC is earned on the PPA (because subsection 127(9) includes the PPA in "qualified expenditures"), the PPA cannot be included in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the actual overhead expenses that the PPA represents are deducted as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1) of the Act.

body.text: 3.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, and the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule

Salaries and wages represent the core of most Canadian SR&ED claims. Under the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and subsection 248(1) of the Act, "salary or wages" means the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act, including all fees received for services not rendered in the course of the taxpayer's business, but excluding superannuation or pension benefits and retiring allowances.

General inclusions in SR&ED salary or wages comprise base salary and wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips, gratuities, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, inducement payments and non-competition payments to employees, bonuses and remuneration based on profits (strictly for employees other than specified employees), and taxable benefits under section 6 where the value is a reasonable estimate of actual employer cost excluding any GST/HST or PST. Under subsection 248(16), any GST/HST input tax credit (or provincial PST credit/rebate) that an employer can claim on employee taxable benefits is deemed to be government assistance and must be excluded from allowable SR&ED salary or wages. Conversely, general exclusions from SR&ED salary or wages include dividends paid to founders, the employer's share of payroll-related benefits, extended vacation or sick leave, stock option benefits under section 7 (excluded for options granted or shares issued on or after November 17, 2005), retiring allowances, and unpaid remuneration under subsection 78(4). Under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), if the portion of time an employee spends directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada is all or substantially all (90% or more), 100% of their eligible salary expenditure is deemed to be for SR&ED.
For specified employees (and for the calculation of the Proxy Method salary base more broadly), the Act and Regulations impose strict statutory limitations:

headers: Technical Rule & Impact on SR&ED Claim

cells: Exclusion of Bonuses & Profit-Based Pay from Direct Claim
Bonuses and remuneration based on profits incurred for specified employees are completely excluded from SR&ED salary or wages (both for the Section 37 pool and Section 127 ITC).
Associated Group Allocation of Specified Employee Salaries

Where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, the associated corporations must file Form T1174 to allocate the allowable salary or wages of the specified employee among the group.
Exclusions from the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base

Even though allowable as direct SR&ED salaries on Line 306, the following are excluded from the Part 5 salary base used to compute the 55% PPA: (1) all taxable benefits (s. 6); (2) all bonuses; (3) all remuneration based on profits; (4) extended vacation/sick leave; and (5) prior-year unpaid amounts paid in the current year (Line 310).
Proxy Salary Base Caps for Specified Employees (75% & 2.5 × YMPE)
Under the Proxy Method, the salary base for a specified employee is further capped at 75% of time spent on SR&ED and at a maximum of 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE).

Accrued salary or wages not paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not incurred in that year, and can only be claimed in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (on Line 310, excluded from the proxy base). (Reasonable vacation/holiday pay and statutory salary deferral arrangements are deemed paid on the 180th day, but are excluded from the proxy base.)

body.text: 3.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

Under the Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(a) (Traditional Method), and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method), a claimant may deduct and claim ITCs on the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

"Materials for SR&ED" refer strictly to physical and tangible raw materials, substances, or other items (in solid, liquid, or gaseous states) that compose the body of a tangible object at a given moment in the SR&ED process—either a tangible object on which SR&ED is carried out or that results from SR&ED. Expenditures to purchase equipment, data, or software licences are expenditures of a capital nature and do not qualify as materials. Materials may be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers, provided they are used directly in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada and paid for within 180 days of the end of the taxation year under subsection 127(26). The claimable amount is the laid-down cost (invoice price, customs and excise duties, transportation, acquisition, and storage costs); for items drawn from the claimant's self-manufactured inventory, cost includes the laid-down cost of materials, direct manufacturing labour, and a reasonable portion of production overhead. If materials are purchased from a non-arm's length (NAL) entity, subsection 127(11.6) restricts the ITC-eligible cost to the cost incurred by the NAL supplier (adjusted selling cost), excluding any intercompany profit element.

CRA policy distinguishes between materials consumed (materials destroyed or rendered virtually valueless during SR&ED, which are not subject to ITC recapture unless proceeds received exceed 10% of cost) and materials transformed (materials incorporated into a prototype, pilot plant, or experimental batch that retains commercial value, which are subject to ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) to (36) if sold or converted to commercial use). Energy and water generally do not qualify as materials when used to operate equipment, heat buildings, wash floors, or feed boilers. However, energy qualifies as a material when it becomes an integral part of a chemical reaction/conversion process or where the energy source itself is the subject of SR&ED, and process water qualifies as a material consumed if it enters the process and becomes part of intermediate or final products as governed by chemical equations (outside commercial production).
3.4 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant pays external parties to perform SR&ED in Canada, the tax treatment depends on whether the expenditure is an arm's-length SR&ED contract, a non-arm's length (NAL) SR&ED contract, or a third-party payment.

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), payments to an arm's-length contractor to perform basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible support work in Canada on behalf of the claimant are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool (reduced by any related expenditure of the performer that is not of a current nature, except for post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs made by the performer). For Section 127 ITC purposes, since 2013 only 80% of the eligible contract expenditure qualifies as a "qualified expenditure" under subsection 127(9). Furthermore, the payment must be made to a "taxable supplier"—defined in subsection 127(9) as a person resident in Canada, a Canadian partnership, or a non-resident/non-Canadian partnership that receives the amount in the course of carrying on business through a permanent establishment in Canada (defined in Regulation 8201). Amounts paid to a contractor that is not a taxable supplier are completely excluded from qualified expenditures and earn 0% ITC.

If a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) party (defined in section 251), the payment is deductible in the payer's Section 37 pool, but subsection 127(24) excludes the payment from the payer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. Instead, the NAL performer may transfer all or part of its own qualified SR&ED expenditures (subject to the non-arm's length adjusted service cost rules in subsections 127(11.6) to (11.8)) to the payer by jointly filing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) under subsections 127(13) to (16) (with the performer reporting the transferred amount on Line 540 and the transferor on Line 546 of Form T661). If an arm's-length contractor subcontracts work back to a party not dealing at arm's length with the payer, the deemed contract payment rule in subsection 127(25) applies.

By contrast, third-party payments under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii) are payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, approved associations, granting councils (Entities B to E), corporations resident in Canada (Entity A), or tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations resident in Canada under paragraph 149(1)(j) (Entity F), where the third party controls the research (typically basic or applied research) and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results in its Canadian business. Third-party payments are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool, 80% includable in qualified expenditures for the Section 127 ITC (when paid to a taxable supplier), and require filing Form T1263. Payments in kind (property or services provided to a university or college) are valued at fair market value (FMV) provided there are no conditions requiring direct or indirect payments back to the claimant, and third-party payments cannot be used to acquire a building, a leasehold interest in a building, or pay building rent (paragraph 37(8)(d)).

body.text: 3.5 Overhead and Other Expenditures (Traditional Method Only) and Cloud Computing

Claimants that elect the Traditional Method may claim "overhead and other expenditures" on Line 360 of Form T661. Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the Act and paragraphs 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3)(a)–(b) of the Income Tax Regulations, general accounting overhead under GAAP is not automatically allowable. Instead, an expenditure (or a reasonable portion thereof) qualifies as SR&ED overhead only if it satisfies both tests set out in the SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022):

items: The Directly Related Test: There must be a direct linkage—with no intervening step or intermediary—between the expenditure and (i) the SR&ED work, (ii) the SR&ED staff, or (iii) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED.
The Incremental Test: The expenditure (or portion thereof) would not have been incurred if the prosecution of SR&ED (or the provision of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment) had not occurred.

body.text: Applying these two tests to specific industrial and technology expense categories establishes clear boundaries. First, cloud computing and software subscriptions are claimable on Line 360 only under the Traditional Method, where they are directly related and incremental to the SR&ED work; if claimed under the Proxy Method, they are automatically disallowed. Second, fixed monthly telephone, cellular, and internet subscription payments are non-incremental ordinary business expenses and do not qualify regardless of employee time spent on SR&ED, whereas identifiable incremental costs (such as long-distance telephone charges) qualify under the Traditional Method. However, under the CRA's updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), applying the Tax Court precedent in Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1877), costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for dedicated bandwidth are allowed even under the Proxy Method as a lease of equipment (because bandwidth relies on underlying optoelectronic equipment, which is not GPOEF). Third, for clerical and administrative staff, salary or wages are allowable on Line 360 under the Traditional Method only if there is a direct linkage to non-technological services aiding ongoing SR&ED and the cost is incremental; related benefits, retiring allowances, training costs, and travel expenses for clerical/administrative staff have only an indirect link and are disallowed. For hands-on SR&ED employees, by contrast, the employer's share of related benefits, retiring allowances, moving/relocation expenses (subsection 62(3)), training costs in Canada, and travel/lodging expenses in Canada for customer-location testing are directly linked and allowable under the Traditional Method. Fourth, non-SR&ED contract costs directly supporting SR&ED, utilities, maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment (Regulation 2900(3)(a)), periodical subscriptions, clinical study volunteer fees, and incremental waste disposal during active SR&ED projects also qualify under the Traditional Method.
3.6 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures and equipment lease costs were statutorily excluded from the SR&ED program. Bill C-15 reversed this exclusion, restoring eligibility for both SR&ED capital expenditures (depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, i.e., on or after December 16, 2024) and equipment lease costs (incurred after December 15, 2024). The CRA published three updated policies in May and June 2026 governing these rules: the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), the SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), and the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026).

For SR&ED Capital Expenditures reported on Line 390 of Form T661 (with the 10 most expensive assets and their operating-time percentages detailed on Lines 262 and 263), eligibility is governed by paragraph 37(1)(b), subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) (Traditional Method), and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III) (Proxy Method). To qualify, the property must be depreciable property (subsection 13(21)) acquired after December 15, 2024, where at the time of acquisition the claimant intended that either (1) the property would be used during all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or (2) all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value would be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (such as property used in developing a prototype or pilot plant that has less than 10% life expectancy or less than 10% value remaining after development, or is used in other SR&ED afterwards). Under subsections 37(1.2) and 127(11.2) (in conjunction with subsections 13(26), 13(27), and 248(19)), capital property is deemed not acquired until it becomes available for use—creating a technical opportunity noted by tax practitioners where equipment purchased on or before December 15, 2024, but not delivered and available for use until after December 15, 2024, may qualify. Capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 are deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) and must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (CCA) unless the claimant fails to claim them by the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline. For assets not claimed under SR&ED, Bill C-15 also enacted a 100% first-year CCA deduction for Classes 44, 46, and 50 acquired after April 15, 2024 and available for use before 2027 (alongside Class 12 purchased application software at 100%), and suspended the half-year rule with a 3 times normal first-year allowance for other property acquired after 2024 and available before 2030 (and 2 times from 2030 through 2033).

When new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 does not meet the 90% ASA intent test because it is used for both SR&ED and commercial production, it may qualify on Line 504 (Box 792) of Form T661 as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under subsection 127(9) and Regulation 2900(11). Unlike the ASA test (which evaluates intended use over the asset's useful life), the SUE test evaluates actual operating time during two statutory periods. If the equipment is new (never used or rented before acquisition), is not GPOEF, is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11)(c)–(d) (which excludes equipment intended at acquisition to be used during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing/processing facility, plant, or line and used primarily for non-SR&ED over its useful life), and is actually used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada during the first period (from the available-for-use date to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time), it qualifies as First-Term SUE, deeming 25% (1/4) of its capital cost (excluding borrowed money under section 21 and adjusted for NAL costs under subsection 127(11.6)) to be a qualified expenditure for the ITC. If it continues to be used primarily (>50% to <90%) for SR&ED during the second period (from the available-for-use date to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time), it qualifies as Second-Term SUE for an additional 25% (1/4) of its capital cost. SUE capital cost is excluded from the Section 37 pool and is depreciated on Schedule T2SCH8, with any SUE ITC applied or refunded reducing the UCC of the CCA class in the subsequent year.

body.text: 3.7 Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits

To ensure SR&ED tax incentives subsidize only the net economic cost of R&D rather than commercial assets or inventory sold for revenue, subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Act impose SR&ED ITC Recapture (Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, updated October 14, 2022).

Recapture is triggered when all four statutory conditions under subsection 127(27) are met: (1) the claimant acquired a particular property from a person or partnership in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 preceding years to 20 preceding years by subsection 127(36) for ITCs earned in 1998 and subsequent years); (2) the cost of the property was claimed as a qualified expenditure; (3) a percentage of that cost can reasonably be considered to have been included in computing the claimant's ITC; and (4) in the current taxation year, the claimant disposes of (sells) the property (or another property that incorporates it) or converts it to commercial use.

When triggered, the recaptured ITC is added directly to federal Part I income tax payable for the year of sale or conversion (reported on Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) and is then added back to the claimant's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the following taxation year under paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and (c.3). For materials transformed and ASA capital property, the recapture equals the lesser of (i) the ITC originally earned on the property, and (ii) the original ITC rate multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (for an arm's-length sale) or the fair market value (FMV) of the property (for a conversion to commercial use or a non-arm's length disposition). For Shared-Use Equipment (which is considered converted to commercial use only if SR&ED use becomes incidental, i.e., ASA converted to commercial use), the second prong applies the original ITC rate to 25% of the proceeds/FMV (if only First-Term SUE was claimed) or 50% of the proceeds/FMV (if both First- and Second-Term SUE were claimed)—for example, if equipment acquired for $160,000 earned $28,000 in First- and Second-Term SUE ITCs at 35% and is later sold for $100,000, the recapture is the lesser of $28,000 and 35% × ($100,000 × 50%) = $17,500.

body.text: 4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentives (2026 Landscape)

Nine Canadian provinces and one territory (Yukon) layer their own corporate R&D tax credits on top of the federal SR&ED program, while three jurisdictions—Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut—do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit. Except for Québec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration [TRA]), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the CRA on behalf of the provinces and are claimed on provincial schedules filed with the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return.
4.1 Ontario (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Ontario administers three distinct corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all harmonized with the federal definition of SR&ED and administered by the CRA. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Taxation Act, 2007) is an 8% refundable tax credit (rate in effect for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016; previously 10%) available to CCPCs with a permanent establishment in Ontario on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (generating up to $240,000 in refundable cash annually). While the federal expenditure limit doubled to $6 million under Bill C-15, Ontario's OITC expenditure limit remains $3 million for 2026. The $3 million OITC limit is shared among associated corporations and phases out when the associated group's prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or when its prior-year taxable paid-up capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Per the CRA T2 Corporation Income Tax Guide, the OITC is claimed by filing Schedule T2SCH566 (Ontario Innovation Tax Credit) alongside Schedule T2SCH3113.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Taxation Act, 2007) is a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (rate in effect for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016; previously 4.5%) available to any corporation with a permanent establishment in Ontario on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (net of any OITC or OBRITC claimed), with no expenditure cap. Unused ORDTC may be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years, and is claimed on Schedule T2SCH508 (Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit) (with transitional debits/credits on Schedules 506/507). Because the ORDTC constitutes government assistance that reduces federal qualified expenditures in the year earned, a corporation in a tax-loss position may elect to renounce (waive) the ORDTC on or before its filing due date to avoid reducing its 35% refundable federal ITC. Additionally, any portion of the ORDTC attributable to the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) must be added to income on Schedule T2SCH1 in the taxation year it is applied to reduce Ontario tax payable.

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Taxation Act, 2007) is a 20% refundable tax credit available to corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment for qualified expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with an eligible research institute (certain post-secondary institutions, hospital research institutions, and prescribed non-profit research organizations). Eligible contract expenditures are capped at $20,000,000 per year (allocated across associated corporations), yielding a maximum refundable credit of $4,000,000 per year. It is claimed by filing Schedule T2SCH568 and Schedule T2SCH569 (entered on Line 470 of Schedule 5).
4.2 Québec (The New CRIC Regime and Replacement of Legacy Credits)

In its 2025–2026 Budget, the Gouvernement du Québec enacted a major reform of provincial innovation taxation under the Taxation Act (Québec), replacing eight legacy R&D and innovation tax credits—including the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7-V, where many claimants previously received a 14% base rate), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V), and the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V)—with a single unified measure: the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC — Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation).

For taxation years or fiscal periods beginning before March 26, 2025, claimants continue to file under the legacy credits alongside Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting SR&ED Expenditures) (and cumulative research consortium fees or dues paid at the end of a taxation year ending after March 25, 2025 may continue to generate consortium credits for a taxation year ending no later than December 31, 2029). For all taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the CRIC applies exclusively to corporations (and corporate members of partnerships) that operate a business in Québec, maintain an establishment in Québec, and undertake (or subcontract) eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Québec. While Québec's R&D definition is harmonized with federal legislation (and the CRA conducts the scientific review of R&D work), the CRIC expands provincial eligibility to cover pre-commercialization activities undertaken in conjunction with R&D work carried out in Québec—specifically: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation; (2) product design, including form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials; and (3) quality control activities, strictly where related to implementing a quality control system required to obtain initial approval or certification.

The CRIC is a 100% refundable tax credit paying 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures that exceed the applicable exclusion threshold, and 20% on qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 maximum. The annual exclusion threshold carved out before applying the 30% and 20% rates is equal to the greater of (1) $50,000, or (2) the sum of the basic personal amount of the applicable personal income tax system for each eligible employee, adjusted to reflect the proportion of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities. Qualified CRIC expenditures comprise 100% of salaries and wages paid to the corporation's employees for eligible work in Québec, 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec, 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity, and 100% of property acquisition costs (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings). A corporation cannot combine the CRIC with another Québec tax credit (such as the C3i investment and innovation credit) on the same expenditure, nor can it claim the CRIC on property used in a large investment project holding a tax-holiday qualification certificate. The CRIC is claimed by filing Form RD-1029.8.CR-T with the Québec corporate income tax return.
4.3 British Columbia

Under Part 6 of the British Columbia Income Tax Act, qualifying corporations with a permanent establishment in British Columbia (including corporate active members of a partnership) may claim the BC SR&ED Tax Credit at a rate of 10% of qualified BC SR&ED expenditures incurred before September 1, 2027. For qualifying CCPCs, the 10% credit is 100% refundable on qualified BC expenditures up to the CCPC's federal expenditure limit. Because the BC legislation ties a CCPC's refundable cap to its federal expenditure limit (which increased from $3 million to $6 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024), practitioner guides note that the refundable BC base extends up to $6 million ($600,000 refundable credit), whereas older CRA summary pages still display the legacy $300,000 maximum based on the former $3 million limit. For non-CCPCs, active corporate partnership members other than CCPCs, or CCPC expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit, the 10% credit is non-refundable and may be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 10 taxation years. Under sections 102.1 to 102.6 of the BC Income Tax Act, disposing of BC SR&ED property or converting it to commercial use within 10 years of acquisition triggers BC SR&ED recapture (reported on Line 241 of Schedule 5). To claim the credit, the corporation must file Form T666 with its T2 return no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year.
4.4 Alberta

Following the elimination of the former Alberta SR&ED tax credit effective January 1, 2020 and the reduction of Alberta's general corporate income tax rate from 12% to 8% under the Job Creation Tax Cut, Alberta introduced the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) effective January 1, 2021 under Section 26.6 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act. In the 2025 Alberta Budget, the province removed the sunset clause, making the IEG a permanent structural component of Alberta's corporate tax system.

Delivered through the Alberta corporate tax system on up to $4,000,000 in annual qualifying Alberta SR&ED expenditures (yielding a maximum annual refundable grant of $800,000), the IEG is 100% refundable and provides: (1) an 8% payment on eligible R&D spending carried out in Alberta up to the corporation's base level of spending, and (2) an enhanced 20% payment on eligible R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's base spending level (alternatively expressed in some practitioner guides as an 8% base credit on all eligible spending up to $4 million plus a 12% incremental credit on spending above the base level). A firm's base level of spending is calculated as its average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the previous two taxation years. The grant phases out incrementally for corporations (and associated groups) with between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital, and corporations with $50,000,000 or more in taxable capital are ineligible. Administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA), the IEG is claimed on the Alberta AT1 return by filing AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29), AT1 Schedule 13, and Form AT4970 (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Claimed in Alberta).
4.5 Saskatchewan

Governed by Section 63.4 of The Income Tax Act, 2000 (Saskatchewan) and administered by the CRA, the Saskatchewan Research and Development Tax Credit provides a 10% credit on qualifying SR&ED expenditures incurred in Saskatchewan. According to Saskatchewan funding documentation (updated June 2026), effective December 16, 2024, the province doubled the annual threshold for the 10% refundable tax credit for CCPCs from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 of qualifying Saskatchewan expenditures (increasing the maximum annual refundable CCPC credit from $100,000 to $200,000, though older CRA summary pages still list the legacy $1 million figure). Qualifying expenditures of a CCPC above the refundable threshold, as well as all qualifying expenditures of non-CCPCs, earn a 10% non-refundable tax credit. Across all corporations, the maximum total annual credit (refundable plus non-refundable combined) is capped at $1,000,000 per corporation per year (reached at $10,000,000 in qualifying expenditures). Unused non-refundable credits can be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 10 taxation years, and the credit is claimed on Schedule T2SCH403.
4.6 Manitoba

Under Section 7.3 of The Income Tax Act (Manitoba), corporations with a permanent establishment in Manitoba earn a 15% Manitoba Research and Development Tax Credit on eligible expenditures made after April 11, 2017 (previously 20%). If the R&D is carried out in Manitoba under an eligible contract with a prescribed post-secondary educational or research institution, the 15% credit is 100% refundable (and 100% of the institutional contract payment is claimable, rather than the federal 80% inclusion). For all other in-house Manitoba R&D, 50% of the credit is refundable (7.5%) and 50% is non-refundable (7.5%), and capital expenditures remain eligible in Manitoba. Unused non-refundable credits can be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years. Under subsection 7.3(7), a corporation may renounce all or part of its credit no later than 12 months after its T2 filing due date. The credit is claimed on Schedule T2SCH380 (entered on Line 606 of Schedule 5 for the non-refundable credit and Line 613 for the refundable credit) within 18 months of the tax year-end.
4.7 Atlantic Provinces (Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Newfoundland and Labrador)

All three Atlantic provinces that offer an R&D incentive provide a 15% fully refundable corporate tax credit with no expenditure ceiling and no restriction to CCPCs, administered by the CRA. Nova Scotia provides a 15% fully refundable credit claimed on Schedule T2SCH340 (Nova Scotia Research and Development Tax Credit), with any property recapture reported on Line 221 of Schedule 5. New Brunswick provides a 15% fully refundable credit (for expenditures incurred after December 31, 2002; legacy non-refundable credits carried back 3 years and forward 7 years) claimed on Schedule T2SCH360 (New Brunswick Research and Development Tax Credit). Newfoundland and Labrador provides a 15% fully refundable credit claimed on Schedule T2SCH301 (for corporations) or Form T1129 (for individuals).
4.8 Yukon and Other Territories

Administered by the CRA, the Yukon Research and Development Tax Credit provides a 15% fully refundable tax credit on eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in Yukon, plus an additional 5% refundable bonus credit (for a combined 20% refundable rate) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University. To claim the credit, a taxpayer must file Schedule T2SCH442 (Yukon Research and Development Tax Credit) with its return no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year. Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit.
4.9 Intellectual Property (IP) Box Regimes and Federal Patent Box Status

While the federal government consulted on a proposed federal patent box (a tax break rewarding companies for keeping Canadian inventions and IP in Canada) in 2024 and included it in its 2025 election platform, the federal government omitted the patent box from both the November 2025 Federal Budget and the 2026 legislative cycle. Consequently, Canada has no federal patent box in force as of November 2026. At the provincial level, OECD and government records confirm two active provincial IP box regimes: (1) Québec's Deduction for Incentive for the Commercialization of Innovations (DICI — Déduction incitative pour la commercialisation des innovations), introduced effective January 1, 2021 (for which the 2025–2026 Québec Budget legislative notes confirm that the Québec nexus ratio is not reduced by the new CRIC exclusion threshold), and (2) Saskatchewan's Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (SCII), introduced in 2017 and updated in 2024, which provides a corporate income tax rate reduction on qualifying technology commercialization income.

body.text: 5. Interaction with Government Assistance, Grants, and Contract Payments
5.1 Statutory Framework for Assistance and Contract Payments

A core principle of Canadian R&D tax law is that a taxpayer can claim SR&ED tax incentives only on its net out-of-pocket R&D expenditure. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) (for the Section 37 deduction pool) and subsections 127(9), 127(11.1), 127(18), and 127(19) (for Section 127 qualified expenditures), any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its income tax return filing due date for the taxation year reduces its SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar.

In subsection 127(9), government assistance is defined as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (including Crown corporations, foreign governments, and indirect government funding delivered via non-profit organizations) in the form of a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance, other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself. Crucially, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (such as Ontario's OITC and ORDTC, Québec's CRIC, BC's SR&ED credit, Saskatchewan's R&D credit, and Alberta's IEG) are legally classified as government assistance and reduce both the Section 37 pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures in the year earned, unless formally renounced on time where permitted. Non-government assistance is defined in subsection 127(9) as any amount that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) (without reference to subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(v) to (vii)) received as an inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance toward property cost or an outlay/expense.

A contract payment under subsection 127(9) is an amount paid or payable to a claimant by a taxable supplier (for SR&ED performed for or on behalf of a person or partnership entitled to deduct it) or by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or Part I tax-exempt entity for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf. A contract payment reduces the performer's Section 127 qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar so that both parties cannot claim an ITC on the same work, whereas it does not reduce the performer's Section 37 deduction pool. If a firm develops technology on its own account (bearing the financial cost) and later uses it on client engagements, the client fees are not contract payments for SR&ED, provided engagement contracts support that separation. Where assistance and contract payments relating to a project exceed the claimant's own SR&ED expenditures on that project, the excess reduces the qualified expenditures of any non-arm's length party working on the project under subsection 127(19), allocated using Form T1145 under subsection 127(20). Conversely, if a claimant repays government or non-government assistance or contract payments in a subsequent year, the repayment is added to the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and generates ITCs under paragraphs 127(9)(e.1) and (e.2).
5.2 The Bona Fide "Excluded Loan" Exemption (Bill C-69, Royal Assent June 20, 2024)

Historically, low-interest or interest-free repayable innovation loans issued by federal or provincial public authorities created uncertainty over whether the loan principal constituted "government assistance" under subsection 127(9). To resolve this issue, Bill C-69, which received Royal Assent on June 20, 2024, amended subsection 127(9) of the Act to state that bona fide loans with reasonable repayment terms from public authorities in Canada—defined as an "excluded loan" in subsection 12(11)—are generally not government assistance, retroactively effective January 1, 2020 for loans made after December 31, 2019. Consequently, unconditionally repayable government loans with reasonable repayment terms do not reduce a claimant's Section 37 SR&ED pool or Section 127 qualified expenditures. By contrast, forgivable loans, non-repayable grants, and emergency wage subsidies (such as the former Canada Emergency Wage Subsidy and 10% Temporary Wage Subsidy) remain government assistance that reduce SR&ED claims dollar-for-dollar.
5.3 Stacking Mechanics with Key Canadian Innovation Grants

Canadian R&D performers routinely stack non-dilutive direct grants with post-facto SR&ED tax credits, subject to two overarching constraints reported in funding guides: (1) direct grants reduce the SR&ED expenditure base dollar-for-dollar, and (2) across federal and provincial programs, total combined government assistance (grants + federal SR&ED + provincial R&D credits) generally cannot exceed 75% of total eligible project costs.

Suppose a CCPC conducts a 9-month SR&ED project employing two senior engineers at $125,000/year each (spending 100% of their time on the project for 9 months, or 75% of a full year), resulting in $187,500 in total eligible SR&ED salary costs. 6.2 Statutory Reporting Deadlines and the Absolute Bar on Extensions

Under subsection 37(11) (for deducting SR&ED expenditures) and paragraph 127(9)(m) (for earning an ITC), a claimant must file the prescribed forms (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) containing all prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred.

For corporations, because the T2 return filing due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) is 6 months after the end of the taxation year, the SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year. For example, if a corporation's taxation year ends on December 31, 2025, its T2 return is due June 30, 2026, and its SR&ED claim must reach the CRA on or before June 30, 2027; on July 1, 2027, the credit for that year is permanently lost. For individuals, the reporting deadline is 17.5 months from the end of the taxation year. For trusts (whose T3 return is due 90 days after year-end under paragraph 150(1)(c)), the reporting deadline is 12 months after the trust's filing due date (e.g., March 30 of the second following year for a December 31 year-end). For partnerships, Form T661 must be filed with the T5013 Partnership Information Return no later than 12 months after the earliest of all filing due dates for the return of income of any member for the tax year in which the partnership's fiscal period ends. When a reporting deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognized public holiday, the claim is on time if received or postmarked on or before the next business day; for electronic filing via Corporation Internet Filing, the filing date is the date the confirmation number is issued.

Under subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12), paragraph 127(9)(m), and subsection 220(2.2) of the Act, the SR&ED reporting deadline is absolute. Subsection 220(2.2) prohibits the Minister of National Revenue from extending the deadline to file prescribed SR&ED forms, and the taxpayer relief provisions in subsection 220(3.1) (and books-and-records provisions in section 230) provide no relief or extension for late SR&ED claims. Under subsection 37(12), if the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information are not filed by the reporting deadline, the expenditure is not considered an expenditure on or in respect of SR&ED—precluding both deduction in the Section 37 pool and earning an ITC under Section 127. Furthermore, once the reporting deadline has passed, a claimant under review cannot amend its claim to add new projects, add missing prescribed information, or substitute additional expenditures to make up for amounts disallowed by the CRA.
6.3 The Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

Introduced in the Canada Strong Budget 2025 following Winter 2026 consultations and launched by the CRA on April 1, 2026, the Pre-Claim Approval Process is an optional upfront technical evaluation allowing eligible businesses to confirm whether their planned work meets the definition of SR&ED before beginning the project or incurring significant costs.

To qualify for Pre-Claim Approval, the business must (1) be a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC), another Canadian corporation, or a Canadian partnership; (2) have an annual gross business income of less than $25,000,000; and (3) be in good standing with the CRA. In addition, the proposed project must (4) not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim (the application must be submitted before starting work or when work has only recently begun, and cannot be used as a retrospective year-end remedy), and (5) not involve issues currently under litigation.
Eligible businesses apply through a four-step procedure:

items: Request a Case Number: Complete a 5-minute online web form (providing province/territory, contact name, phone number, business name, and Business Number). Existing SR&ED claimants in good standing are contacted within 2 business days through My Business Account; all other businesses are contacted within 5 business days by phone with a case number.
Submit the Application in My Business Account: Upload the completed application and existing project documentation in My Business Account for up to 3 proposed projects.

Meet with a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA): Within 4 weeks of submitting the application, the CRA assigns an RTA. For new SR&ED claimants, attending a 2-to-5-hour meeting (which may include a virtual or on-site tour of the premises) with the RTA and the company's technical expert is mandatory; for existing claimants in good standing, the meeting is optional at the CRA's discretion. At the close of the meeting, the RTA provides a verbal summary of the uncertainty, planned systematic investigation, and recommendations.

Receive Written Determination Within 8 Weeks: Within 8 weeks of receiving the completed application in My Business Account, the RTA issues a written Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report. If approved, the pre-claim approval is valid for up to 3 years. If pre-claim approval is not granted, there is no formal objection process, though the business may request a new case number and re-apply if it makes material changes to the project, or proceed to file a standard post-year-end SR&ED claim.
