body.text: 6.4 CRA Technical and Financial Review Process and Dispute Resolution Hierarchy

When a filed Form T661 is selected for review, the review follows the CRA's updated guide, The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026). The review is conducted jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who evaluates whether the work meets the eligibility requirements and reports to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who reviews the claimed expenditures and reports to Financial Review Management [FRM]).

In Step 1 (The Start of the Review), one of the assigned reviewers contacts the claimant by phone to provide the names and contact details of the RTA and FR, confirm the official language of choice, identify the specific projects and issues selected for review, and schedule a virtual (or exceptionally, on-site) review meeting. The reviewer follows up with an initial letter summarizing the call, providing a meeting agenda, contact information for the reviewers and their managers, and any pre-meeting information requests—which generally carry a 30-day deadline under Standard Timelines for Information Requests. In Step 2 (The Review Meeting and Requests for Additional Information), the RTA and FR interview the company's technical and financial personnel, conduct a virtual or on-site tour of the premises, inspect contemporaneous supporting evidence (design documents, hypotheses, test results, source code history, scrap/artifacts, timesheets, payroll, contracts, and proof of payment), and share preliminary findings at the end of the meeting. In Step 3 (The End of the Review), the RTA prepares an SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, and if adjustments are proposed, the FR issues a proposal package (including the eligibility report and a proposal letter detailing proposed adjustments and any penalties), giving the claimant generally 30 days to respond with written representations and new supporting facts or documents.
If a claimant disagrees with how the review is conducted or with the review findings, the CRA's Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns establish a four-tier escalation hierarchy:

items: Step 1 — Talk with the Reviewer(s): Discuss concerns and submit written representations directly to the assigned RTA and FR.
Step 2 — Talk with the Manager(s): If unresolved with the reviewers, escalate the dispute to the RTA's Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or the FR's Financial Review Management (FRM).

Step 3 — Request an Administrative Review: If concerns remain unresolved after speaking with the reviewers and managers, request an Administrative Review upon receipt of the proposal package. An Administrative Review is not a second technical review of the claim by different reviewers; its purpose is strictly to verify that the review was conducted in accordance with SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures, and to confirm that the claimant was accorded due process.

Step 4 — Formal CRA Notice of Objection (and Tax Court Appeal): Once the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, a claimant that disagrees with the final decision has the statutory right to file a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, followed by an appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.

body.text: 6.5 Claim Preparer Penalties (Subsection 162(5.1)) and Gross Negligence Penalties (Subsection 163(2))

To police compliance across the SR&ED program, the Income Tax Act enforces two distinct statutory penalty provisions. First, in Part 9 of Form T661, the corporation must disclose whether a paid external claim preparer assisted in preparing the claim (employees preparing the claim as part of their employment duties are not claim preparers), and report who the preparer is, their billing arrangement (contingency percentage, hourly, or flat fee), the rate, and the total fee paid or expected (for example, reporting a 25% contingency fee on a $160,000 credit as a $40,000 fee). Under subsection 162(5.1) of the Act, if required claim preparer information is missing, incomplete, or false, a $1,000 penalty per SR&ED claim applies, for which the claimant corporation and the claim preparer are jointly liable.

Second, under the CRA's updated Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (published January 28, 2025; formerly Application Policy SR&ED 96-05), any person who knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence (beyond a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act), makes, participates in, agrees to, or accepts the making of a false statement or omission in an initial or amended SR&ED claim is subject to a civil penalty under subsection 163(2). Under subsection 163(3), the CRA bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities ("more likely than not").
The CRA policy identifies six specific situations where it will consider applying the gross negligence penalty on an SR&ED claim:

items: The claimant participated in the overstatement of amounts on which SR&ED tax incentives are being claimed;
The claimant included amounts for a project despite clear evidence that they knew the project did not involve SR&ED activities;
The claimant described SR&ED activities that did not take place (or did not take place in that year) and claimed normal business expenses as SR&ED expenditures;
The claimant continued to claim non-qualifying amounts after being advised in writing that they do not qualify (and the amounts are not under objection or appeal);
The claimant continued to miscalculate SR&ED tax incentives after being advised in writing of the correct calculation; or
The claimant continued to claim unsubstantiated SR&ED amounts after being advised in writing what documentation is required to support them.

body.text: Under subsection 163(2), the gross negligence penalty for an overstated SR&ED claim is the greater of $100 or 50% of the total of (1) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (paragraph 163(2)(a)), plus (2) the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed by the claimant (paragraph 163(2)(d)). Under subsection 163(2.1), if a claimant reports a net loss, taxable income is deemed not to be less than zero when computing the tax understatement on personal or false expenses. Furthermore, when a gross negligence penalty applies to the refund of a refundable ITC under paragraph 163(2)(d), the CRA calculates the 50% penalty on the entire overstated refund claimed, regardless of whether a portion of the overstatement was caused by a simple oversight. In the policy's worked example for an overstated ITC deducted against Part I tax at the 35% enhanced rate, a claimant that knowingly claims $200,000 of normal commercial salary as SR&ED salary (plus $20,000 of general materials by simple error) generates $200,000 of knowingly overstated salary plus $110,000 of overstated 55% PPA ($310,000 total overstated qualified expenditures), yielding an overstated ITC of 35% of $310,000 = $108,500 and a 50% gross negligence penalty of $54,250.
7. Landmark Jurisprudence and Judicial Precedents Governing SR&ED in Canada

Because subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED through broad principles, Canadian tax courts have established the binding legal standards governing technical eligibility, the scientific method, and evidentiary sufficiency.
7.1 Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC)

Decided by Judge (later Chief Justice) Donald Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada, Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen is the foundational judicial authority on SR&ED in Canada. Reviewing Information Circular IC 86-4R3 (dated May 24, 1994) and calling it a generally useful and reliable guide, Judge Bowman established five criteria (at paragraphs 14–16) for determining whether an activity constitutes SR&ED.

First, on technological risk or uncertainty, Judge Bowman held that the uncertainty must not be removable by "routine engineering or standard procedures," which he defined as "techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field". Second, on the formulation of hypotheses, Judge Bowman outlined a five-stage process: (a) the observation of the subject matter of the problem; (b) the formulation of a clear objective; (c) the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (d) the formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (e) the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses. Third, on the scientific method, Judge Bowman required that the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method—characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses—noting that while intuition, creativity, and genius may play a crucial role, they must operate "within the total discipline of the scientific method," and cautioning that what appears routine and obvious after the event may not have been obvious before the work was undertaken. Fourth, the process must result in (or aim at) a technological advancement. Fifth, a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results must be kept as the work progresses.
7.2 RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132 (FCA)

In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, the Federal Court of Appeal approved Judge Bowman's Northwest Hydraulic criteria as binding appellate law across Canada and confirmed that systematic research includes testing. Crucially, at paragraphs 14 and 15 of RIS-Christie (as subsequently applied by the Tax Court in Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 42 at para. 118, Les Abeilles at para. 94, and National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 at paras. 65–66), the Federal Court of Appeal clarified the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion (contemporaneous records). Because a detailed written record of hypotheses and test results is not explicitly required by the text of the Income Tax Act or Regulations, it is not mandatory in law that the evidence be documentary, and credible testimonial (oral) evidence is acceptable—though failing to maintain adequate contemporaneous documentation carries severe practical litigation risks if oral testimony fails to prove systematic testing.
7.3 C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393

In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (at paragraph 17), the Federal Court of Appeal summarized Judge Bowman's Northwest Hydraulic framework into the canonical five questions applied in subsequent Canadian SR&ED cases:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?
Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses?
Did the process result in a technological advancement?
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: 7.4 Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355

In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, a thermoformed plastic products manufacturer appealed the disallowance of its 2005 SR&ED claim for developing proprietary "Multi-Bins". Justice D'Arcy's decision at the Tax Court (unanimously affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal) established two key principles. First, at paragraph 3, Justice D'Arcy placed no weight on the testimony of the CRA's Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) because the Crown called him as a fact witness rather than qualifying him as an expert witness, and most of an RTA's testimony regarding SR&ED eligibility constitutes inadmissible opinion evidence. (Similarly, in 2011 TCC 391, the Tax Court criticized a CRA expert report whose primary purpose was merely to justify the reviewer's prior 2004 disallowance of battery-charger projects.) Second, on the merits, the Court dismissed Jentel's appeal because the taxpayer failed to demonstrate a systematic investigation through experiment or analysis performed to resolve any scientific or technical uncertainties.
7.5 Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 246, aff'd 2021 FCA 88

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, a metal stamping company appealed the denial of its 2009 and 2010 SR&ED claims. After the Tax Court (2019 TCC 246, per Justice Owen) found that the taxpayer failed the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion (adherence to the scientific method), Kam-Press argued before the Federal Court of Appeal (2021 FCA 88, decided May 10, 2021, per Justice Webb) that because the definition of SR&ED had been moved from the Regulations to subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and contained no reference to the words "scientific method", the Tax Court erred in applying the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion.

The Federal Court of Appeal unanimously rejected this argument. Citing its prior decisions in RIS-Christie (1998), C.W. Agencies (2001), Jentel Manufacturing (2011), and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. (2016), the FCA held that the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) was not materially different from the former regulatory definition, and reaffirmed that adherence to the scientific method is a mandatory requirement for SR&ED eligibility in Canada.
7.6 National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47, aff'd 2022 FCA 72

In National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, an SR&ED consulting firm claimed SR&ED credits for developing the "PTS Project," a computer program designed to automate portions of filing SR&ED claims with the CRA. Both Justice Lafleur at the Tax Court (2020 TCC 47) and Justice Rennie at the Federal Court of Appeal (2022 FCA 72, decided May 2022) dismissed the appeal. Reaffirming Kam-Press Metal Products, the Federal Court of Appeal held that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria are the settled interpretation of subsection 248(1), and upheld the trial judge's finding that developing software using existing computer languages where the obstacles encountered are normal programming problems—and where the claimant did not conduct its work in a methodical manner or keep adequate records—does not constitute SR&ED.
7.7 Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 32

In Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 32), the Tax Court of Canada ruled in favour of the taxpayer across seven disputed food-manufacturing SR&ED projects spanning the 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2016 taxation years (involving $343,449 in denied expenditures and $60,963 in denied ITCs across 2013, 2015, and 2016, plus three disallowed 2014 projects). Canafric developed new frozen pie recipes and production processes for major food retailers (such as Costco and Loblaws). Relying on the Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies five-criteria framework, the Tax Court held that the evidence and testimony provided by Canafric's CEO (Mr. Pandya) satisfied all five criteria for systematic experimental testing and formulation, allowing the claimed SR&ED expenditures and ITCs in full.

body.text: 8. Strategic Compliance Framework and Audit Readiness Checklist

To maximize recovery under the expanded 2026 SR&ED regime while protecting claims against CRA audit disallowances and subsection 163(2) penalties, businesses and tax advisors should implement the following two operational governance matrices adapted from 2026 CPA practitioner frameworks:
8.1 Nine-Stage Professional SR&ED Filing and Audit Governance Checklist

headers: Mandatory Technical, Financial, and Statutory Review Actions

cells: • Confirm taxation year-end, T2 due date (6 months), and absolute 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline (ITA s. 37(11), 127(9)(m)). • Verify corporate status: CCPC, Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC), or non-CCPC. • Ensure founders performing hands-on R&D are paid via salary/wages (not dividends, which add nothing to the salary base) and pay all accrued bonuses/wages within 180 days of year-end (ITA s. 78(4)). • For businesses with <$25M gross business income, evaluate applying for the CRA's optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (launched April 1, 2026) before starting work on up to 3 projects.

• Document every project around the 2021 CRA Guidelines' "Why" requirement (scientific or technological uncertainty + advancement sought) and "How" requirement" (hypotheses formulated + systematic experiment/analysis + logical conclusions). • Clearly separate technological uncertainties from business problems or routine software/engineering delivery. • Establish exact project completion dates (eligibility ceases when uncertainty is resolved) and link all Paragraph (d) support work directly to Canadian core experimental work.

• Reconcile T4 payroll, segregate specified employees, remove specified employee bonuses and profit-based remuneration (ITA s. 37(9)), and apply the 2.5 × YMPE and 75% proxy salary base caps (ITR s. 2900(7)–(8)). • Verify permissible foreign SR&ED employee wages meet all 5 statutory conditions and cap at 10% of Line 306 (ITA s. 37(1.4)–(1.5)). • Separate materials consumed from materials transformed. • Verify all arm's-length contractors are Canadian taxable suppliers (80% ITC inclusion) and execute Form T1146 for any non-arm's length contracts. • Reconcile post-December 15, 2024 capital equipment (Line 390), Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504), and equipment leases.

• Compare the 55% Proxy Method (ITR s. 2900(4), testing the A − B − C overall proxy cap) and the Traditional Method (Line 360 incremental overhead + Section 37 pool addition) for the taxation year. • Elect Traditional Method if incremental cloud compute or shop-floor overhead exceeds 55% of the salary base; otherwise elect Proxy Method on Line 160 (remembering the election is irrevocable for that filed year).

• Calculate the $6,000,000 enhanced 35% expenditure limit (post-Dec 15, 2024 tax years). • Model the $15M to $75M phase-out across the associated/consolidated group: for CCPCs with prior-year taxable capital >$15M but lower 3-year average gross revenue, evaluate electing the 3-year average gross revenue test ($15M–$75M). • File Schedule T2SCH49 to allocate the expenditure limit among associated CCPCs.

• Track physical location of R&D staff, labs, and subcontractors across provinces using province-specific project codes and logs. • Calculate provincial credits first (Ontario OITC/ORDTC/OBRITC, Québec CRIC, BC Form T666, Alberta IEG, Saskatchewan/Manitoba/Atlantic/Yukon) and deduct provincial assistance and direct grants (NRC IRAP) sequentially from the federal base. • Consider renouncing non-refundable Ontario ORDTC or Manitoba R&D credit if in a persistent tax-loss position.

• Complete the May 2026 revisions of Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (plus T1145, T1146, T1174, T1263, and provincial schedules) and reconcile to the T2 return and financial statements. • Ensure Line 207 (5-digit Statistics Canada CRDC code "RDF#####"), Lines 212/214 (Pre-Claim Approval case number), Lines 262/263 (top 10 post-Dec 15, 2024 capital assets and operating-time %), and Part 9 (claim preparer fee disclosure) are completed to avoid the $1,000 s. 162(5.1) penalty.

• Organize technical records, dated hypothesis logs, failed trial evidence, source code repository history, employee project timesheets, contractor statements of work, invoices, proof of payment within 180 days, and operating-time logbooks for post-Dec 15, 2024 capital equipment, SUE, and leased equipment; identify technical and financial leads who will explain the claim to the RTA and FR.

• Record assessment/reassessment dates (90-day Notice of Objection window). • Monitor 20-year ITC carryforward pools, Section 37 indefinite deduction pools, paragraph 37(1)(e) / 12(1)(v) prior-year ITC inclusions, subsection 37(6.1) loss restriction events prior to M&A closings, and the 20-year ITC recapture window (ITA s. 127(27), (36)) on materials transformed, capital equipment, and SUE.

cells: 1. Claiming commercial delivery work as research
The claim is reduced or denied on technical eligibility under ITA s. 248(1) (National R&D, Kam-Press).
State the technological uncertainty in a single clear sentence before claiming the project.
2. Confusing a business problem with a technological uncertainty
Project is disallowed on audit and taints the credibility of the remainder of the claim.
Ask whether a competent professional in the field could have resolved the problem using standard practice or routine engineering.
3. Missing client funding, contract payments, or grants
Reassessment disallowing the ITC with arrears interest (often years later) and potential 50% gross negligence penalties under ITA s. 163(2).
Identify and reconcile every grant and client receipt against each project before computing qualified expenditures under ITA ss. 37(1)(d) and 127(18).
Claimed hours are reduced by the CRA Financial Reviewer to what can be objectively supported or disallowed.
Track employee hours at the project level from the day the project opens.
5. Claiming cloud compute under the Proxy Method
The cloud compute expenditure is automatically disallowed on audit because overhead is replaced by the 55% PPA.
Choose the calculation method deliberately on Line 160; cloud compute belongs strictly to the Traditional Method (Line 360).
6. Using the outdated 65% or 60% proxy rate
Overstated credit is corrected on assessment; repeated miscalculation after written CRA notice can trigger penalties.
Apply the statutory 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount rate of the salary base under Income Tax Regulations subsection 2900(4).
The associated group exceeds an expenditure limit it was legally required to share.
